edits.find:
Bottom line

Read the plain film by site and periosteum; then recall what that lesion does next.

  • Painless hard bump near a joint, spur continuous with the cortex and medulla: osteochondroma. It grows until the physes close, then stops. Observe; no biopsy. About 1% of solitary lesions turn malignant.
  • Night pain relieved by NSAIDs (nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs), small lucent nidus: osteoid osteoma. It involutes over years.
  • Central metaphyseal lucency, no periosteal reaction: unicameral bone cyst. Observe with serial films; the risk is fracture.
  • Sunburst periosteum, often with a Codman triangle, in a metaphysis: osteosarcoma. Onion skin in the shaft, pelvis or spine, sometimes with fever: Ewing sarcoma.

Night pain that wakes the child, with fever or weight loss, points to malignancy, not a benign lesion.

An aggressive film gets MRI (magnetic resonance imaging) before biopsy; chest CT (computed tomography) stages the lungs. Fever does not exclude a tumor: Ewing sarcoma can raise the ESR (erythrocyte sedimentation rate), CRP (C-reactive protein) and WBC (white blood cell count).

edits.find:
Bottom line

After a foot puncture, the exposure and the clock name the organism:

  • First 1 to 4 days, spreading redness: cellulitis from Staphylococcus aureus or streptococci.
  • Nail through a shoe, pain and redness persisting a week or more, little fever, often a normal WBC (white blood cell count): osteomyelitis or osteochondritis (bone or cartilage infection) from Pseudomonas aeruginosa, carried in from the shoe's foam sole.
  • Wound soaked in fresh water at injury (NBME adds soil), then a fast-spreading infection: Aeromonas hydrophila. Salt water: Vibrio vulnificus.

A normal film does not exclude bone infection; MRI (magnetic resonance imaging) does better. Treat with debridement and bone culture, covering Pseudomonas and S. aureus.

edits.find:
Bottom line
  • Head tilts toward a firm sternocleidomastoid mass that appears at 1 to 4 weeks and does not transilluminate, chin turned away: congenital muscular torticollis; the muscle bends the head toward itself and turns the chin away. Clinical diagnosis; stretching, repositioning, tummy time and physical therapy. Late treatment leaves permanent craniofacial asymmetry.
  • Flat occiput, ear on that side forward (parallelogram): positional plagiocephaly, from supine sleep, a neck that turns one way or prematurity. Reposition; no imaging.
  • Flat occiput, ear pushed back with a ridge (trapezoid): lambdoid craniosynostosis. Head CT (computed tomography) and craniofacial referral.

Breech, oligohydramnios or twins (intrauterine crowding): examine the hips and feet; hip dysplasia, metatarsus adductus and clubfoot travel with torticollis.

A new tilt in an older child with any neurologic sign is a posterior fossa tumor until MRI (magnetic resonance imaging).

edits.find:
Bottom line

Bilateral leg pain in a child: examine before you test.

  • Normal exam, episodic evening or night pain with pain-free days, age 3 to 12: growing pains. Reassure; no labs or films.
  • Tender calves days after an influenza-like illness: benign acute childhood myositis (influenza-induced myositis). CK (creatine kinase) is high and reflexes are preserved.
  • Ascending weakness with absent reflexes: Guillain-Barré syndrome.
  • Bone tenderness with pallor, bruising, fever or weight loss: CBC (complete blood count) with smear for leukemia.
  • One side, a focal tender spot or a mass: radiograph, even when night pain responds to NSAIDs (nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs).

Night pain alone is not the flag; laterality, a limp, tenderness and systemic signs are.

Myositis can cause weakness (the NBME explanation: mild weakness to quadriparesis), so strength does not separate it from Guillain-Barré syndrome; preserved reflexes do, with calf tenderness and a high CK in support.

edits.find:
Bottom line

A Marfanoid child: look for what Marfan does not do.

  • Intellectual disability, a thrombotic stroke or clot, fair skin and hair, lens dislocated down: homocystinuria. Plasma homocysteine and methionine are both high.
  • Normal intellect, lens up and out, aortic root dilation: Marfan syndrome. Echocardiographic surveillance and a beta-blocker or angiotensin receptor blocker.
  • Stretchy skin, easy bruising and lax joints with normal proportions: Ehlers-Danlos syndrome, not a Marfanoid disorder.

Treat homocystinuria with pyridoxine (B6) first (about half respond), plus folate and vitamin B12 (cobalamin); nonresponders need methionine restriction and betaine. Never nitrous oxide.

edits.find:
Bottom line

A contusion whose pain clears, then returns weeks later with a firm, mobile intramuscular mass, is myositis ossificans: bone forming inside the muscle (quadriceps and brachialis most often).

The exam decides it:

  • Pain on passive stretch of the muscle (knee flexion for the quadriceps)
  • Strength and sensation intact
  • No fever, erythema or limb-wide swelling

Early films are often normal; calcification appears at about 4 to 8 weeks. Never biopsy an early lesion: it can mimic osteosarcoma.

Treat with range of motion and an NSAID (nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drug) such as indomethacin; excise only a mature lesion that stays symptomatic.

edits.find:
Bottom line

A septic hip is a surgical emergency: aspirate before antibiotics.

Count the Kocher criteria:

  • Fever over 38.5 °C
  • Refuses to bear weight
  • ESR (erythrocyte sedimentation rate) over 40 mm/h
  • WBC (white blood cell count) over 12,000/mm³
  • CRP (C-reactive protein) over 2.0 mg/dL is often added as a fifth

3 or more: blood culture and ultrasound-guided aspiration. 0 or 1: transient synovitis; NSAIDs (nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs) and a recheck.

An effusion, and the flexed, abducted, externally rotated hip it causes, occurs in both septic arthritis and transient synovitis; effusions in both hips favor transient synovitis.

Septic fluid (over 50,000 WBC/mm³, neutrophil-predominant) means surgical drainage plus IV antibiotics.

Set the subtype by the first 6 months:

  • In every intentional overdose, check acetaminophen and salicylate levels, and suspect more than one substance
  • Then name the toxidrome from the pupils, the skin, the bowel sounds and the muscle tone
